questions.q: What two functions do you combine to plot a circuit's state on a Bloch sphere?
options: plot_histogram and AerSimulator
Statevector and plot_bloch_multivector
transpile and plot_state_city
QuantumCircuit and plot_histogram
questions.explain: You build a Statevector from the circuit, then pass it to plot_bloch_multivector, which draws one Bloch sphere per qubit.

questions.q: Where does the state |0> (no gates applied) sit on the Bloch sphere, and where does |1> (after qc.x(0)) sit?
options: Both at the same point
|0> at the north pole (0,0,1), |1> at the south pole (0,0,-1) — exact opposites
|0> on the equator, |1> at the north pole
Both on the equator but at different longitudes
questions.explain: Verified Bloch vectors: |0> maps to (0,0,1), the north pole; |1> maps to (0,0,-1), the south pole. X flips the vector straight through the center of the sphere.

questions.q: After qc.h(0), the Bloch vector is verified as (1, 0, 0). What does this tell you about the H gate's effect?
options: H moves the state to the south pole
H leaves the state unchanged
H sends the state to the equator, along the +x axis — the geometric picture of equal superposition
H has no defined Bloch vector
questions.explain: (1,0,0) sits exactly on the equator (z=0), maximally far from both poles, which is the geometric meaning of an equal-superposition state like |+>.

questions.q: qc.ry(math.pi/3, 0) gives a verified Bloch vector of (0.866025, 0, 0.5) — y=0 throughout. What does this confirm about RY rotations?
options: RY rotates within the y-z plane
RY rotates within the x-z plane, since the vector never leaves y=0
RY has no effect on the Bloch vector
RY always moves the vector to a pole
questions.explain: RY(theta) rotates the Bloch vector within the x-z plane. Starting from the north pole (0,0,1) and rotating 60 degrees toward +x lands exactly at (sin60, 0, cos60) = (0.866025, 0, 0.5), matching the y=0 plane.

questions.q: qc.rx(math.pi/2, 0) gives a verified Bloch vector of (0, -1, 0) — x=0 throughout. Which plane does this confirm RX rotates within, and how does that differ from RY?
options: RX rotates within the x-z plane, same as RY
RX rotates within the y-z plane, a different plane than RY's x-z plane
RX and RY rotate within the same plane but opposite directions
RX has no defined rotation plane
questions.explain: The resulting vector (0,-1,0) has x=0 throughout, confirming RX(theta) rotates within the y-z plane, distinct from RY's x-z plane rotation — each rotation gate is named after the axis whose plane it rotates within.
